periods.activity_title: Awakening the Senses: Pre-Reading and First Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.28): paired recall of a sensory visit, writing five details.
Let us read (p.28): short oral share — how the memory feels, and imagining sight/hearing loss.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to shut their eyes briefly and name one thing they can feel, smell, or hear in the room right now. Briefly introduce Helen Keller — a writer who navigated the world without sight or hearing — and orient students to the essay's central question: what would you most want to see if given three days of sight?

Students work in pairs on the pre-reading task under “Let us read” (p.28): recall a place they visited and note down the name, companions, and one detail for each of the five senses. Teacher circulates and prompts where a sense is left blank.

A quick paired exchange on the follow-up prompts from “Let us read” (p.28): how the memory feels, and whether the experience would differ without sight or hearing. Two or three pairs share aloud; teacher notes recurring ideas on the board.

Teacher reads the essay aloud from p.28 to p.30 at an unhurried pace, pausing after each paragraph to ask one open question — “What does Keller mean here?” Students follow in their textbooks and may mark words they find interesting.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading pairs surface what students already know about sensory experience, giving Keller’s argument a personal anchor before the text opens. A common difficulty is that students treat the pre-reading as a quick list exercise; encourage genuinely specific sensory words rather than generic labels like “nice smell”.

periods.activity_title: Completing the Read and Checking Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss I (p.31): identify the true statements from a set of seven about the essay.
Let us discuss II (p.32): complete the three-day table with Keller’s planned activities.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss III (p.32): write two to three sentences on how the narrator understands a person’s feelings without sight.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads p.30–31 of the essay aloud, covering Keller’s account of the second and third days. Students follow in their books; teacher pauses after each day’s account to check that students can name what Keller wanted to do.

Students work individually on the true-statements task under “Let us discuss I” (p.31), selecting the four correct ones from the seven given. Pairs then compare answers before a whole-class check, with teacher guiding the class to cite the exact lines that support or disprove each statement.

Pairs complete the three-day table from “Let us discuss II” (p.32), filling in Keller’s planned activities for each day. Teacher invites one pair per day to read out their entry; the class adds or corrects details.

Teacher sets the homework question from “Let us discuss III” (p.32) and reads it aloud so students know what is expected: two to three sentences explaining how Keller understands a person’s feelings through touch.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the essay together, the true/false task now asks students to move from recall to textual evidence — a step many students skip by guessing. Insist on a page reference for every verdict. The three-day table consolidates the essay’s structure and is the factual foundation the analysis tasks later build on.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Language, Tone and the Touch of Nature

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect I, Extract 1 (p.32): tone, texture phrases, symbolism, and fill-in on Extract 1.
Let us think and reflect I, Extract 2 (p.33): word choice, ‘sleeping earth’, purpose of ‘should’, and fill-in on Extract 2.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 — the passage on the delicate symmetry of a leaf and the quiver of a singing bird — aloud expressively from p.32 while students follow. Ask one student to name the feeling the passage creates before moving to analysis.

Students work through the four questions under “Let us think and reflect I, Extract 1” (p.32): identifying the symbolism of the leaf, listing texture phrases, completing the sentence about ‘awakening Nature’, and selecting the tone. Teacher takes responses in sequence and uses wrong tone choices to discuss the difference between nostalgic, proud, admiring and celebratory.

Teacher reads Extract 2 — the passage beginning with the dawn of the second day — aloud from p.33, then asks students why Keller uses the phrase ‘sleeping earth’ before distributing attention to the printed questions.

Students tackle the four questions under “Let us think and reflect I, Extract 2” (p.33): MCQ on ‘thrilling’, the sleeping-earth question, the fill-in on Keller’s purpose, and the repeated use of ‘should’. Teacher leads a brief whole-class debrief, drawing out that ‘should’ signals conditional, wishful planning rather than obligation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Keller’s account of the first two days together, students are now attending to language rather than plot — a shift that sometimes feels unfamiliar. Anchor every literary question in a specific phrase from the extract so students see that analysis means looking closely at chosen words, not summarising the paragraph. The repeated-‘should’ question is the most conceptually demanding; allow students to read the extract again quietly before discussing it.

periods.activity_title: Reflective Discussion: Values, Advocacy and Gratitude

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.33): discuss Keller’s advocacy for mindful senses and what her three-day choices reveal about her values.

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: “Keller says we should use our eyes as if tomorrow we might be struck blind. What would you do differently today if you believed that?” Allow students to respond freely to warm up the reflective register.

Teacher leads a structured discussion of the first three extended-response questions under “Let us think and reflect II” (p.33): how touch compensates for lost sight and hearing, why Keller considers sight the most wonderful sense, and how her argument could make us kinder toward people with different abilities. Students share ideas in pairs first, then with the class.

Whole-class discussion of the final three questions from “Let us think and reflect II” (p.33): the significance of imagining sense-loss, how Keller encourages mindful sensory engagement, and what her three-day choices reveal about her values and priorities. Teacher records key phrases on the board as a shared note.

Brief closing reflection: each student writes one sentence summarising the most important thing Keller’s essay made them think about. Teacher invites two or three students to read their sentences aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having analysed Keller’s language in Extract 1 and Extract 2, students are now moving to the essay’s wider argument and its implications for how we live. Students tend to produce thin answers to value-based questions; push them to anchor every claim in something specific Keller wrote or a day she planned. The final one-sentence reflection serves as a formative signal and does not need to be collected or marked.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Inclusion, Speaking of Our Senses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.36): select four true statements from seven after hearing the Anuj–mother conversation.
Let us speak (p.36): speak for a minute on the sense you value most, using the given prompts.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening activity: tell students they will hear a conversation between a boy named Anuj and his mother about a classmate who uses Braille and about Digital India’s assistive technologies. Ask students to keep the seven numbered statements on p.36 open and tick or cross each as they listen.

Teacher reads the conversation aloud at a natural pace from p.41–42 (students do not look at the transcript). Teacher reads it a second time; students finalise their four true-statement selections from “Let us listen” (p.36). Pairs compare choices; teacher leads a brief whole-class verification, explaining why each incorrect statement fails the transcript.

Transition to speaking: teacher reads the prompt list under “Let us speak” (p.36) aloud and models a short response about one sense, demonstrating how to use the scaffolded sentence starters without simply listing them.

Students prepare briefly in silence, then pairs take turns to speak for a minute each on their chosen sense. Teacher circulates, offering a quiet prompt to students who stall. Two or three volunteers share with the class; teacher affirms specific details and sense-language that stood out.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task places Keller’s personal advocacy in a present-day school context through Anuj’s conversation, which helps students connect the essay’s ideas to their own experience. A common difficulty in the listening task is students confusing statements 3 and 4; clarify that statement 3 is confirmed by Anuj’s own words, and statement 4 requires reading what the mother says about screen readers. For the speaking task, gently discourage students from simply reading the prompt list aloud — the goal is a connected, personal response.
materials: Textbook p.36 (student page), transcript p.41–42 (teacher copy)

periods.activity_title: Descriptive Paragraph: Writing a Place Through the Senses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.37): plan, draft, and revise a descriptive paragraph of a visited place using all five senses.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the three-part structure — attention-grabbing opener, sensory supporting lines, and a closing impression — by writing two or three sentences about a familiar place on the board, naming the device (alliteration, simile, or personification) used in each line. Students note which sense each detail appeals to.

Students plan their own descriptive paragraph using the guidelines under “Let us write” (p.37): they choose a place they visited and jot down one sensory detail for each of the five senses before writing a word for the opening line and the closing impression.

Students draft their paragraph. Teacher circulates, prompting for specific details wherever a student has written a vague phrase such as “it smelled nice” and encouraging the use of at least one literary device in the supporting lines.

Pairs exchange drafts and give one piece of feedback each: name the strongest sensory detail and suggest one place where a more specific word or a literary device would strengthen the paragraph. Students revise the identified line before the sitting closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The descriptive paragraph task is grounded in the essay’s central sensory argument: Keller’s own vivid descriptions — the delicate symmetry of a leaf, the happy quiver of a singing bird — serve as implicit models. Students often front-load visual details and neglect smell, taste, and touch; prompt them to include at least one non-visual sense in the supporting lines. Every piece of writing should begin and finish within these minutes so no student carries an incomplete draft out of the room.

periods.activity_title: Sensory Words and Modal Verbs in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn I (p.34): complete sensory-word table from the text and add new words in Column 3.
Let us learn II–III (p.34): identify modal verbs in five sentences and label each function from the given box.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn IV (p.35): fill in seven blanks with appropriate modal verbs and write the function of each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces sensory vocabulary: explain that descriptive writing depends on words that appeal to one or more of the five senses, and that good writers choose these words deliberately. Ask students for one sensory word each from Keller’s essay as a warm-up.

Students complete the sensory-word table under “Let us learn I” (p.34): they scan the essay for at least one word per sense for Column 2 and add a new word of their own in Column 3. Pairs compare and discuss; teacher verifies the Column 2 answers against the text before moving on.

Teacher introduces modal verbs, writing the five functions from the box on the board (possibility, necessity, polite request, ability, moral obligation) and offering one quick example sentence for each. Clarify that the same modal verb can carry different functions depending on context.

Students underline the modal verb in each of the five sentences under “Let us learn II–III” (p.34) and write the function beside it. Teacher conducts a quick oral check sentence by sentence, inviting students to justify their function label.

Teacher sets the homework fill-in task from “Let us learn IV” (p.35) and reads the first sentence aloud with the class, modelling how to decide which modal fits the stated function before students complete the rest independently at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The sensory-word table draws directly from Keller’s essay — words like ‘panorama’, ‘perfume’, ‘rough’, and ‘relish’ appear there — so students can verify their Column 2 answers by returning to the text rather than guessing. Students often confuse ‘possibility’ and ‘ability’ when labelling modals; illustrate the difference with ‘can’ in two distinct sentences before the check.

periods.activity_title: Braille, Disability Awareness and Inclusive Mindset

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore I (p.37–38): study the Braille code and write your name using bindis or daal grains.
Let us explore II (p.38): find out when and how India observes the International Day of Persons with Disabilities and write findings on a display sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly explains that Braille is a tactile script where each letter is a pattern of raised dots, and that it is named after Louis Braille. Point out the Braille code chart on p.37–38 and ask students to identify one or two letters before starting the activity.

Students work individually on the Braille task under “Let us explore I” (p.37–38): they use the code chart to transliterate their name into Braille dot patterns and represent the dots using bindis, daal grains, or pencil marks on paper. Teacher circulates and checks that students are reading the cell patterns correctly.

Students work in pairs for the research and writing task under “Let us explore II” (p.38): using any available reference (textbook, teacher briefing, or printed fact sheet provided by the teacher) they note when the International Day of Persons with Disabilities falls (3 December) and at least two ways it is observed in India, then write their findings neatly on a sheet for the class board.

A few pairs read their findings aloud; teacher invites the class to add any detail not yet mentioned. Teacher closes by connecting the activity back to Keller’s essay: inclusion is not just the right tools, but also the right mindset — echoing the mother’s words in the listening transcript.

periods.teacher_notes: The Braille activity is experiential and tactile, which directly mirrors Keller’s argument that touch is a rich sensory channel. Prepare bindis or a small packet of split daal at the start of the sitting so the hands-on work can begin immediately; students who wish to use pencil marks instead are equally welcome. For the disability-awareness task, have a brief printed fact sheet on hand in case internet access is unavailable.
materials: Bindis or split daal / small grains
Plain paper or card for Braille names
Optional: printed fact sheet on International Day of Persons with Disabilities

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: From Keller’s Vision to Our Own

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a two-question oral synthesis: “Keller uses touch to understand the world — which single sensory detail from her essay did you find most powerful, and why?” and “How does the Anuj–mother conversation update Keller’s idea of inclusion for today?” Students respond in pairs; three or four pairs share aloud.

Quick vocabulary recall: teacher reads eight words drawn from across the chapter — sensory words from “Let us learn” and modal verbs from the essay — and students write the word’s sense-category (sight / hearing / touch / smell / taste) or the modal’s function beside each. Pairs check each other’s answers.

Students write an original short paragraph — eight to ten sentences — responding to the following prompt: “If you were given three days of a sense you do not currently have, which sense would you choose, and what would you do with it?” They must use at least two sensory words and one modal verb and apply the three-part structure practised in the descriptive paragraph — attention-grabbing opener, specific supporting details, closing impression.

Students pair up and read their paragraphs to each other, then each names the one detail they found most vivid in their partner’s writing. Teacher invites two or three volunteers to share with the class. Teacher closes by returning to Keller’s final appeal: to see, hear, touch, smell and taste as if every experience might be the last — a charge the chapter has spent its time building towards.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together Keller’s sensory argument, the vocabulary of the five senses, the modal verb work, and the inclusive ideas raised by the Braille and Digital India material — all of which form the chapter’s content across its sections. The writing prompt asks students to inhabit Keller’s imaginative method rather than summarise it, which makes the task genuinely generative. Every piece of writing in this sitting begins and ends within these minutes.
materials: Textbook (any page students wish to consult)

items.item_stem:
Helen Keller describes how she would spend each of the three days if she were granted sight. Read the statements below and write True or False for each. If the statement is False, correct it in one short phrase.
1. On the first day of sight, Keller would spend her time visiting museums to trace the history of humankind.
2. Keller compares the eye to a ‘window of the soul’ because she believes it reveals a person’s true feelings more completely than touch can.
3. On the third day, Keller would stand at a busy city corner to observe people going about their ordinary lives.
4. Keller concludes her essay by urging sighted people to be grateful for hearing alone, calling it the most delightful sense.

options.text: Keller compares the eye to a ‘window of the soul’ because she believes it reveals a person’s true feelings more completely than touch can.
Keller concludes her essay by urging sighted people to be grateful for hearing alone, calling it the most delightful sense.
On the first day of sight, Keller would spend her time visiting museums to trace the history of humankind.
On the third day, Keller would stand at a busy city corner to observe people going about their ordinary lives.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — on the first day Keller would see the people whose kindness had enriched her life, not visit museums (museums come on the second day). 2. True — Keller explains that without sight she knows friends only by the feel of their faces and cannot read the subtleties the eye communicates. 3. True — Keller writes that on the third day she would stand at a busy corner watching people and reading smiles, suffering, and determination on their faces. 4. False — Keller urges readers to use all their senses mindfully and concludes that sight, not hearing alone, must be the most delightful sense.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to an informational text by identifying explicit details, interpreting language choices, and reflecting on the author’s argument using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Helen Keller’s three-day sight plan, sensory imagery, ‘window of the soul’, tone, and advocacy for mindful sensory engagement.
items.item_stem: In her essay, Helen Keller makes a passionate appeal to sighted readers: use your eyes as if tomorrow you might be struck blind, and apply the same urgency to every other sense. Drawing on Keller’s argument in the essay, explain in a short paragraph (4–6 sentences) why she believes that imagining the loss of a sense is important, and how this belief shapes the advice she gives to people who can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Keller argues that most sighted people take their senses for granted because they have never had to live without them; imagining sense-loss forces a person to recognise the extraordinary value of what they possess. This recognition, she believes, transforms passive experience into active, grateful engagement with the world. She therefore urges readers to treat every sensory moment as if it could be their last, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and tasting with full attention and appreciation.

items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discuss Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and the mindset needed for true inclusion of visually impaired persons.
items.item_stem:
In the conversation between Anuj and his mother, several ideas about Digital India and assistive technology are exchanged. Choose the correct answer.

Anuj’s mother explains that Digital India is important for visually impaired people primarily because it

options.label: A
options.text: offers assistive technologies such as screen readers and voice-over-enabled smartphones that allow independent use of digital services

options.label: B
options.text: provides free Braille books to schools across the country

options.label: C
options.text: replaces traditional classroom teaching with online video lessons for all students

options.label: D
options.text: trains visually impaired students to become computer programmers

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests a confusion between Braille (the tactile script Anuj notices in Tara’s books) and what Digital India actually provides; the mother never mentions free Braille books.
what_each_option_reveals.D: An over-specific inference; the mother mentions IT and banking as job fields that open up, but does not say visually impaired students are trained as programmers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates Digital India with a general e-learning scheme; the conversation focuses on inclusion of persons with disabilities, not a wholesale shift in classroom teaching.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a spoken conversation and identifies accurate information, distinguishing confirmed from unconfirmed claims using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discuss Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and the mindset needed for true inclusion of visually impaired persons.
items.item_stem: At the end of the conversation, Anuj’s mother says: “Remember, inclusion is not just about having the right tools, but also the right mindset.” In one to two sentences, explain what she means by ‘the right mindset’ and give one example from the conversation that shows either Anuj or his mother demonstrating this mindset.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The right mindset means genuinely accepting and valuing people with disabilities as capable and equal, not simply providing them with technology. Anuj demonstrates this at the end of the conversation when he says he is proud of his school for having facilities for visually impaired students, showing that his attitude toward Tara has shifted from curiosity to admiration and respect.

items.item_stem: Think about the sense you value the most — sight, hearing, touch, smell, or taste. Describe a specific personal experience in which that sense made a memorable difference to you. Speak for about one minute, explaining what happened, what you felt, and why that experience makes you grateful for that sense.

expected_elements: Names a specific sense and a real personal experience clearly.
Uses at least two descriptive or sensory words in the account.
Explains why the experience made the sense feel valuable or irreplaceable.
Speaks in connected sentences without reading from a script.

items.item_stem: Helen Keller argues that people who have never lost a sense rarely appreciate it fully. Do you agree? Speak for about one minute giving your opinion with at least one reason drawn from your own life or from the world around you, and say what you think people could do differently to be more grateful for their senses.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion agreeing, disagreeing, or partly agreeing with Keller.
Supports the opinion with a personal or observed example.
Suggests a concrete action people could take to be more mindful of their senses.
Maintains a confident and connected delivery with a recognisable opening and closing.

items.item_stem: Write a descriptive paragraph about a market, garden, or fair you have visited. Your paragraph must have: (1) an opening sentence that grabs the reader’s attention and introduces the place, (2) at least four supporting sentences that describe what you could see, hear, smell, taste, and touch there, and (3) a concluding sentence that gives your final impression of the place. Include at least one simile or alliteration in your supporting sentences.

expected_elements: Opening sentence is vivid and names the specific place.
At least four senses are represented in the supporting sentences.
One simile or alliteration is correctly and naturally used.
Closing sentence provides a distinct final impression, not a summary of details.

items.item_stem: Helen Keller imagines what she would most want to see, hear, and feel if she could experience the world for only three days. Inspired by her way of thinking, write a descriptive paragraph about an ordinary place — a kitchen, a classroom, a street corner, or a field — as if you were discovering it for the very first time with all your senses fully awake. Make the familiar feel extraordinary. Use your own words and at least one personification in your description.

expected_elements: Chooses a specific, named ordinary place and treats it as newly discovered.
Includes details for at least three different senses, not only sight.
Uses one personification correctly and with clear effect.
The writing conveys a sense of wonder or heightened attention, not just a list of facts.

items.source_context: Sensory words from Keller’s essay (panorama, perfume, rough, relish, music) and modal verbs expressing possibility, necessity, ability, moral obligation, and polite request.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are inspired by Helen Keller’s essay. Each sentence contains a modal verb (given in parentheses). Write one sentence explaining what function the modal verb serves in that sentence: possibility, necessity, ability, moral obligation, or polite request.

(a) A person who has never seen a sunrise (might) not truly understand how Keller felt standing at her window with new eyes.
(b) We (ought to) be more attentive to the small sensory pleasures of everyday life, just as Keller urges us to be.
(c) (Could) you describe what the busiest street in your city looks like to someone who has been blind from birth?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) ‘might’ expresses possibility — it is uncertain whether a sighted person who has never reflected on a sunrise would understand Keller’s feeling. (b) ‘ought to’ expresses moral obligation — it suggests a duty to be more attentive, not merely a suggestion. (c) ‘Could’ expresses a polite request — the speaker is courteously asking someone to perform the action of describing.

items.source_context: Braille script and its tactile dot-pattern system; International Day of Persons with Disabilities and its observance in India.
items.item_stem: Helen Keller’s essay celebrates the sense of touch as a gateway to understanding the world. Braille is a writing system that relies entirely on touch. Using the Braille code, write the word SENSE in Braille dot patterns in the space provided (draw each cell as a 2×3 grid of dots). Then write one sentence explaining what the experience of reading by touch tells you about Helen Keller’s world.

expected_elements: Braille cells for S, E, N, S, E are attempted using the code chart.
Dot patterns are laid out as 2×3 grids, not as random marks.
The sentence draws a genuine connection to Keller’s tactile experience of the world.
Response shows the student has engaged with the Braille task rather than described it abstractly.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of the text’s theme through a hands-on tactile experience and an awareness-raising research task, using interdisciplinary extension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Braille script and its tactile dot-pattern system; International Day of Persons with Disabilities and its observance in India.
items.item_stem: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities is observed on 3 December each year. Design a short awareness campaign for your school to mark this day. In a paragraph of six to eight sentences, describe: (a) what your campaign would be called, (b) two activities you would organise and how each connects to the idea of inclusion, and (c) one thing you would ask your classmates to do differently in daily life as a result of the campaign. Draw on ideas from Helen Keller’s essay and from what you have found out about how this day is observed in India.

expected_elements: Campaign has a clear, relevant name linked to disability awareness or inclusion.
Two specific activities are described with a clear connection to inclusive values.
One concrete, feasible daily-life change is proposed for classmates.
Response draws on Keller’s ideas or facts about the day’s observance in India.
